title: Identify and support learners with special needs

lessons.title: Recognising learners with special needs
lessons.html:
Who are learners with special needs?

In equine and farm training, you may coach riders, train new grooms or run therapeutic riding sessions. Some learners have needs that, without support, make it harder for them to learn. These are sometimes called barriers to learning. South Africa's policy of inclusive education, set out in Education White Paper 6, aims to remove these barriers rather than exclude the learner.

Types of barriers

TypeExamples
PhysicalCerebral palsy, limited mobility, amputation, chronic illness
SensoryVisual impairment, hearing loss or Deafness
LearningDyslexia, dyscalculia, attention difficulties (ADHD)
Intellectual and developmentalDown syndrome, autism spectrum
Emotional and behaviouralAnxiety, trauma, aggression, withdrawal
Social and economicPoverty, hunger, long travel, language of instruction not the home language

Spotting signs

You are not expected to diagnose. Observe and note patterns:

  • Difficulty following spoken instructions, or always watching others first.
  • Avoiding reading or writing tasks; poor spelling far below other work.
  • Poor balance or coordination beyond what is expected.
  • Squinting, holding material very close, or turning the head to hear.
  • Strong reactions to noise or change in routine.
  • Frequent absence, tiredness or hunger.

What to do

  1. Talk privately and respectfully with the learner (and parents for children). Many learners know what helps them.
  2. Check any existing records or medical information, kept confidential.
  3. Refer for specialist assessment where needed, for example to a doctor, psychologist, occupational therapist or the school's support team.
  4. Record your observations objectively.

lessons.title: Supporting learners and adapting your teaching
lessons.html:
Principles of support

  • Respect and dignity: focus on what the learner can do. Use person-first or the learner's preferred language.
  • Confidentiality: share information only with those who need it and with consent.
  • High expectations: adapt the route, not the destination, where possible.
  • Safety: around horses, extra care is needed. Plan for sudden movements and noise.

Adapting teaching

NeedPossible adaptations
Hearing lossFace the learner, use visual signals, written cues, sign language interpreter; agree on arena hand signals
Visual impairmentVerbal description, touch exploration of tack and horse (with a calm horse), large print, consistent layout
DyslexiaDemonstrations, pictures, oral assessment where allowed, extra time
Attention difficultiesShort tasks, clear steps, frequent feedback, fewer distractions
AutismPredictable routine, advance warning of changes, clear literal language
Physical disabilityMounting ramp, adapted saddle, side walkers, accessible facilities

Therapeutic and adaptive riding

Horses can offer real benefits in balance, strength and confidence. Therapeutic riding should be run by trained instructors, with calm, suitable horses, a leader and side walkers, helmets and a doctor's or therapist's clearance.

Working with others

Plan support with parents, therapists, teachers and the learner. Write a simple individual support plan: goals, adaptations, who does what, and review dates.

Evaluating support

Review progress regularly. Is the learner reaching goals? Are adaptations still needed? Ask the learner for feedback.

Key points

  • Barriers can be physical, sensory, learning, emotional or social.
  • Observe and record; refer for specialist assessment, do not diagnose.
  • Respect dignity and confidentiality.
  • Adapt teaching methods, materials and the environment to the need.
  • Plan with the learner, family and specialists and review progress.
